analysis.one_liner: Extends Do Not Call protections to all phone subscribers and lets consumers sue over a single illegal robocall.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2026 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Current Do Not Call rules mainly protect home phone lines, and a 2021 Supreme Court decision narrowed what counts as an illegal auto-dialer. This bill would cover every phone subscriber, let a person sue after just one unwanted telemarketing call instead of two or more, and broaden the legal definition of an automatic dialing system to include machines that dial from a list of numbers. It would also direct the Federal Communications Commission to update its rules to match.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a phone. Under current law, Do Not Call protections apply to residential subscribers, so cell phone users and others get less protection, and violations of the rules are only actionable after repeated calls within a year. The bill extends the rules to all telephone subscribers and allows a private lawsuit after a single call, with actual or punitive damages available [S2]. It also expands the definition of an automatic telephone dialing system to cover systems that dial from a list of numbers successively without human intervention, closing a gap left when courts read the existing definition to exclude list-based dialing [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Removes the word 'residential' from the Do Not Call provisions so the rules cover every telephone subscriber, not just home phone lines [S2].

Changes the private right of action so a subscriber can sue over a single call by an entity, instead of needing more than one call within a 12-month period, and removes the cap language limiting damages in that provision [S2].

Expands the definition of 'automatic telephone dialing system' to include equipment that dials from a list of telephone numbers successively without human intervention, addressing dialing methods courts have held fall outside the current definition [S2].
Directs the FCC to revise its Do Not Call regulations within 270 days of enactment to implement these changes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketers and the automated calling industry. Businesses that call consumers with auto-dialers, including call centers and companies that sell or operate dialing software, would face a wider definition of illegal equipment, exposure to lawsuits after a single unwanted call, and expanded damages [S2]. Some legitimate callers, such as businesses making appointment or service calls with list-based dialing, would also be swept into the stricter rules [S2].

drawbacks.text: The broadened auto-dialer definition and one-call lawsuit standard could expose legitimate callers — appointment reminders, service notifications, or calls to a wrong number — to litigation over a single call [S2].

Removing the 'more than one call' threshold and the 'up to' language on damages increases legal risk for small businesses that use automated calling tools, which could raise compliance costs passed on to customers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real: current law leaves many cell phone users with weaker Do Not Call protection and makes enforcement harder after courts narrowed the auto-dialer definition. The trade-off is that the one-call lawsuit standard and broadened equipment definition could entangle legitimate or mistaken calls in litigation. Stronger FCC rulemaking could mitigate that, but the bill as written leans heavily on private lawsuits as the enforcement mechanism.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent straight to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote since April 2026.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on April 15, 2026, joined by five original cosponsors: Sens. Smith, Hirono, and Welch (Democrats) and Sens. Sanders and King (Independents) [S1].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; the record shows no further action since [S4].
No Republicans have cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no outcome has been reached; telemarketers and automated callers continue operating under the current, narrower rules while the bill sits in committee.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors are Democrats or independents and no Republican has cosponsored, but no opposition vote or statement appears in the record yet.

industries.note: The bill covers all subscribers under Do Not Call rules, allows a lawsuit after a single unwanted call, and broadens the definition of illegal auto-dialing equipment, shrinking the space these callers now operate in. Consumers who receive the calls benefit directly.

industries.industry: Auto-dialer software and call center technology vendors
industries.note: Equipment that dials from a list of numbers successively without human intervention would count as an automatic telephone dialing system, expanding the market for compliant technology and liability for existing tools.

industries.industry: Legitimate business callers (appointments, service and notification calls)
industries.note: Businesses using list-based dialing for appointment or service calls could face one-call lawsuits or new compliance costs, though intentional Do Not Call violators would also be easier to sue.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Commerce Committee with no hearing or markup on the record and no Republican cosponsors. Most consumer-protection bills introduced late in a two-year Congress die in committee without a vote; unless the committee schedules action in the remaining months, it will expire when this Congress ends in January 2027.
